newsitem.title: FRANCE: ALPINE SKIING-NERVOUS ALPHAND EAGER TO TAKE ON ORTLIEB.
newsitem.headline: ALPINE SKIING-NERVOUS ALPHAND EAGER TO TAKE ON ORTLIEB.

text.p: Luc Alphand, the best downhill skier of the last two seasons, is eager to be back in action at last -- weather permitting.

Heavy snow forced organisers to call off the first downhill of the World Cup season in Whistler, British Columbia, last week and similar weather has made practice almost impossible at Val d'Isere this week.
Training was called off on Friday because of bad weather on the OK piste but organisers were hoping that conditions would improve before Saturday's scheduled race.
The Frenchman, World Cup downhill champion for the last two years, has managed only one training run, on Thursday, in between the snowfalls and admitted that delay made him nervous.
"The first race of the season is very important. It tells you where you stand, whether the training sensations were right or wrong," he said.
Thursday's run in Val d'Isere served as a warning for the 31-year-old Alphand who clocked only the seventh fastest time, behind six Austrians led by world champion Patrick Ortlieb.
Alphand knows Ortlieb will be his main rival this season and says the big Austrian is one of the reasons why he keeps on skiing.
"We're not great friends, to say the least. I say hello the first time we meet each year in December and that's it," Alphand said.
"I don't like the way he behaves. Showing off is for him a way to gear up. When he won the world championship last winter he was happy and he showed it. He overdid it a bit"
"So when I start a race, the desire to beat him is also a motivation," he added.

Ortlieb, who has won both the major honours in downhill skiing -- a world crown last winter in Sierra Nevada and Olympic gold in Val d'Isere in 1992 -- made it clear his goal of the season was to take the World Cup away from Alphand.
The easygoing Frenchman's appetite for the duel was increased by an enforced injury layoff before the start of the season.
"I broke my left ankle in September. It was the only part of my legs which had held that far. Then in October, weather conditions made it dificult to train," said the Frenchman.
"I only had six days of real downhill training this autumn. That's why I'm not as self-confident as I was in the past."
The outcome of his showdown with Ortlieb may decide the Frechman's future.
He has repeatedly said he would retire at the end of this season but now hints that he may go on skiing until the 1998 winter Olympics in Nagano.
"I've made up my mind to quit racing at roughly 80 per cent," he said.
If he actually stopped next spring, he would then try to promote his native resort of Serre-Chevalier.
